lessons.title: Plan a search that fits your life

sections.title: A search is a plan, not “any job”

blocks.html:
A job search (Alberta alis often says *work search*) is an organized way to look for work. It is not the same as tapping the first colourful ad you see. Official Canadian pages treat looking for work as a skill you can practise: you decide what you can offer, what you need, and where you will look, then you keep a record of what you have done.

This course cannot promise you a job, a wage, or an interview. It is general information, not licensed career counselling, and not legal, immigration, or Employment Insurance advice. If you need help with a work permit, a claim, or a workplace-rights question, use official Government of Canada or Alberta pages, or ask settlement staff, Alberta Supports, or your adult learning council. Wage-and-hours rules belong in *Alberta Employment Standards information*, not here.

Alis’s *Work Search Basics* page (opened 10 November 2026) says to gather what you need and know what kind of work you want before you start. That includes thinking about your needs and wants in a job — hours you can work, how far you can travel, whether you need a paycheque soon, and what kind of tasks you can do safely. A night warehouse shift is not a good “any job” if you cannot find childcare at night. A job in another city is not a good fit if you cannot move. Write those limits down. They are not excuses. They keep you from spending a week on applications you could not accept.

Alis also distinguishes an occupation (a family of jobs that share skills, such as cook) from a job (one position with defined duties, such as weekend cook at a local hall). You will search with occupation words, then tailor each application to that one posting.

sections.title: Treat the search like work you can organize

blocks.html:
Alis says that when you are looking for work you should be as organized — and as busy — as when you have a paid job. Looking for work is a full-time job for many people, and your performance improves if you keep the details in one place.

Their “master list” can live in a notebook, a Word table, or a simple spreadsheet (the Excel Basics course shows how to keep a list, if you want that skill). Alis says the list should have room for:

  • employer names and contact details, spelled correctly
  • a copy of each job description (postings can disappear before an interview)
  • what you sent (resume, letter, form) and the date
  • application deadlines and interview dates
  • notes about messages you sent or received
  • follow-up tasks, such as a thank-you note
  • the status of each application

Alis also says to name files clearly — for example Sampletown_cover-email_Nov10 instead of Letter — so you do not attach the wrong file. Use a personal email address that you check often, not a current workplace email. Set up voicemail with a clear greeting, because an employer may call when you cannot pick up.

You do not need a fancy app. A paper binder that you can find again is enough. The habit is what matters: every time you apply, you write down what you sent and when.

If you use a public library computer, take your notes with you (or save them to a cloud folder you control) and sign out. Everyday Computers covers locking a shared machine; this course will not walk through device settings again.

sections.title: Know where official help lives

blocks.html:
You will search official sites in the next lesson. Today, know the names so you are not starting from random ads.

The Government of Canada’s Job Bank is a free website for searching jobs across Canada. Alberta’s alis site has a “Look for Work” section with articles on work-search basics, resumes, applying, interviews, and offers. On the alis Look for Work page opened 10 November 2026, the Alberta Supports Contact Centre is listed as toll free 1-877-644-9992. Write that number in your notes if you live in Alberta and want to talk to a person.

Your adult learning council may also run employment-readiness workshops. Ask. Those sessions can include interview practice that this self-paced course cannot watch.

Job Bank has separate resource areas for some groups, including people outside Canada. That is not this course. We will not tell you which immigration category you are in, how to get a work permit, or whether you qualify for EI.

Alis notes that to work in Canada people use a Social Insurance Number (SIN) and that Service Canada issues SINs. This course will not help you apply for a SIN and will never ask you to type one here. When we talk about Job Bank accounts in Lesson 7, you will see that some extra services ask for a SIN — and that you can opt out.

Start this course the way alis starts a search: know what you can offer, know what you need, and get organized. Then look for work that fits that plan, not “any job.”

lessons.title: Find postings on Job Bank and on alis

sections.title: Start with official Canadian job boards

blocks.html:
The Government of Canada’s Job Bank is a free website where you can browse thousands of jobs across Canada. Job Bank’s find-a-job page (opened 10 November 2026) says you can narrow results with filters such as hours of work, benefits, and salary. You can sign up for Job Alerts, a free email service that sends new postings, and you can search on the Job Bank mobile app.

Job Bank also says a search is bigger than one website: you can attend job fairs (online or in person), contact recruiters, and use social media to grow a work network. This basic course will not teach you how to build a LinkedIn profile or how to message strangers safely. Everyday online-safety habits belong in the safety courses; sending email belongs in *Outlook and Workplace Email Habits*. Today the skill is: open an official board, type what you are looking for, and read the list with care.

If a result looks nothing like the hours or town you wrote in Lesson 1, skip it. Filters help, but your own plan still comes first. A salary filter is a search tool, not tax advice and not a promise that the posted number is what you will be paid.

You do not have to create an account to browse many Job Bank postings. Accounts, Job Match, and alerts come in Lesson 7. For now, practise the public search so you can read a list without sharing extra personal details.

sections.title: Search with a title and a place

blocks.html:
A simple Job Bank search uses words an employer might use — a job title or a skill — and a place, such as your town or a nearby city. If your town is small, try the nearest larger centre as well, and be honest about travel (Lesson 1). If the list is long, use a filter that matches your plan, such as part-time hours.

Read more than the first line. Two postings can share a title and ask for very different duties, shifts, or ways to apply. Open the full posting before you decide anything. Write the closing date and how to apply on your master list. Alis reminds people that employers may take a posting down before interviews start, so capture a copy when you are preparing an application — do not rely only on a link.

Screens change. If the live Job Bank page does not match a practice drawing, ask a tutor rather than guessing at a hidden setting. This course will not invent extra buttons. Try more than one wording if the first list is thin — *attendant*, *front desk*, or *weekend* may each surface different ads. If your town returns nothing, add the nearest city you can actually reach, then use the hours filter so weekday-only jobs do not fill the screen. Never type a SIN, a password, or a bank number into a search box. Those facts do not help Job Bank find a shift, and they do not belong in a practice note on a shared computer.

sections.title: Use alis beside Job Bank, not instead of thinking

blocks.html:
Alis is Alberta’s official careers and work-search site. The Look for Work section (opened 10 November 2026) gathers articles on work-search basics, resumes and references, how to apply, interviews, and offers. It is not itself a giant national job board in the same way Job Bank is. Use it to learn how to search and how to prepare, and use Job Bank (and other boards the employer names) to find current postings.

Alis’s work-search basics also say it pays to look at more than one source. Employers sometimes hire through networks, job fairs, or people they already know. You can tell an employer a little about yourself and ask whether your skills might help — without waiting for a posting — if that feels safe and respectful. This course will not ask you to walk into a workplace uninvited or to share private numbers with a stranger.

If you want to talk to a person in Alberta, the Look for Work page lists the Alberta Supports Contact Centre at 1-877-644-9992. Ask your adult learning council as well. Keep using your Lesson 1 plan so a long list of links does not pull you toward work you cannot take.

lessons.title: Read a posting and decide if you can apply

sections.title: A posting is a set of instructions, not a poster

blocks.html:
A job posting tells you what the employer says the work is, what they want, and how they want you to apply. Before you write anything, read it the way you would read a form: slowly, and more than once.

Look for at least these parts:

  • the job title and the employer name
  • the place and the hours or shifts
  • the duties (what you would actually do)
  • the qualifications or required skills
  • assets or “nice to have” items, which are not always required
  • how to apply (email, website form, or in person) and what to attach
  • the closing date, if there is one
  • any notes about pay, which are information — not a promise and not legal advice

Job Bank’s application page says that before you send a resume you should research the company or the job: what the organization does, the duties, the qualifications and skills required, who the customers are, and what reputation the employer has. That research helps you write a resume and letter and prepare for an interview. Use the posting itself, the organization’s website if it has one, and (if it feels safe) people who already work in that kind of place.

Our practice file is a fictional Weekend Attendant role at Sampletown Community Centre. It is marked sample only. It is not a real job and not permission to contact a real town office.

sections.title: Compare the posting with your plan and your skills

blocks.html:
Hold the posting beside the notes you made in Lesson 1. Can you work those hours? Can you get to that place? Are the duties something you can do safely, or learn with the training they offer?

Then compare the required skills with work, volunteering, or daily responsibilities you can honestly describe. Greeting visitors at a front desk is not the same as managing a budget, but it may match a volunteer shift where you welcomed people at a rink. Alis’s work-search basics page (opened 10 November 2026) says that if you think you have the skills to do a job but you do not have all the qualifications, you should not automatically give up. There are ways to format an application so employers can see your abilities. That is not a promise they will overlook a required licence or a legal requirement. It means “missing one asset” is not always the end of the story.

Required items and “assets” are different. A posting that says first aid is an asset is inviting you to mention it if you have it; it is not always a reason to skip the job if you do not. A posting that says you must have a valid class of driver’s licence is a harder line. When you are not sure, ask a tutor or Alberta Supports rather than guessing.

Write a short match list: three things you can show, and anything you cannot. That list will feed the resume (Lesson 5) and the cover email (Lesson 6).

sections.title: Decide: apply, tailor first, or wait

blocks.html:
A careful decision has three common endings:

  • Apply after you tailor a resume and, if they ask, a short letter — because the hours fit and you can show most of the required skills.
  • Tailor first, then apply — you need a day to gather examples and keywords from the posting (Lessons 4–6).
  • Wait or skip — the hours, place, or a hard requirement do not fit, or the posting feels unsafe.

Unsafe signs include a request for a banking password, a fee to “guarantee” a job, or pressure to hide the conversation. Stop and ask council staff. This course will return to careful online applying in Lesson 7. It will not teach you to ignore a scam because you want the work.

Follow the how-to-apply line exactly. If they ask for a resume by email, do not show up unannounced instead. If they ask for a form, fill the form. Alis says to follow the employer’s instructions and preferred format.

lessons.title: Build a master list of your skills and work history

sections.title: A master list is the long version you keep for yourself

blocks.html:
Alberta alis calls this a master resumé: one document that gathers your work experience, skills, accomplishments, and education or training. You do not usually send the whole master list to an employer. You keep it, update it, and copy the most useful parts into a shorter resume for each job.

Alis says a master resume should include your contact information; education and training; work history in reverse order (latest job first), with duties and responsibilities; skills, split into employability skills and technical skills; accomplishments (results you can describe); volunteer and community activities; awards; and a list of references. It is a living document, so you update it when you finish a course, change duties, or complete a volunteer season.

Use a personal phone number with voicemail and a personal email you check often (Lesson 1). You do not have to put a full street address on a practice sheet if you prefer a town name only. Never add a Social Insurance Number, a password, or a bank number. Those do not belong on a resume you would email, and they do not belong in this course.

If typing in Word is new, *Microsoft Word Basics* can help you start a file, save it with a clear name, and check Canadian spelling. This lesson is about what to collect, not about fonts and styles. A lined notebook works too, as long as you can read it later and copy from it without guessing. The point of the master list is speed: when a posting appears, you should not have to rebuild your history from memory on a library computer.

sections.title: Skills, results, and work you might overlook

blocks.html:
Alis asks you to identify skills, abilities, and accomplishments at the beginning of a work search, because that list later feeds both the resume and the interview. Employability skills are everyday workplace habits: showing up, listening, teamwork, speaking clearly. Technical skills are tied to a kind of work: using a till, setting up tables, entering names on a sign-in sheet.

Volunteer work counts when it taught you something an employer needs. Alis’s work-search basics page says not to forget volunteer work. Greeting people at a community skate sale is real public-facing practice, even if it was unpaid. So is keeping a hall kitchen tidy after an event.

Accomplishments are stronger when they include a result. Alis prefers a specific line such as what you did and what changed, rather than a vague claim that you are “great with people.” You do not need a corporate percentage. “Set up twelve tables before a Saturday market, twice a month” is clearer than “helped with events.”

Be honest. If you share a duty with a teammate, say so. Do not invent a job title. If your work history has gaps, you will choose a resume layout in the next lesson; you do not need to fill a gap with a story that did not happen. Daily responsibilities can count when they match a posting — for example, greeting people at a school door as a volunteer, or keeping a written sign-in list at a community supper. Write the task, the setting, and one result, then decide later whether that line belongs on the short resume.

sections.title: References, and how to keep the list usable

blocks.html:
Alis says most employers check references. Choose people who know your work and can speak clearly about it. They should be as objective as you can manage — try not to use a family member if you have another choice. Always ask first, and do not leave this until the night before an interview. It may take time to hear back.

On the master list you can write each person’s name, how they know your work, and whether they have already said yes. You do not have to put reference names on every resume you send; many employers ask later. Follow the posting if it asks for references up front.

Keep the master list where you can find it, with a clear file name. Update it after each new role or course. When you write the short resume in Lesson 5, you will pick only the lines that match that one posting — for our sample, greeting visitors, weekend reliability, and setting up a room, not every job you have ever had.

Ask people you trust to help you remember duties you have forgotten. A second pair of eyes is useful, as long as you do not share other people’s private numbers or a SIN. If you cannot think of a second reference yet, leave that line blank rather than inventing a name. You can add it after someone says yes. Store the worksheet with a name you will recognise, such as master-skills-practice, not Document1.

sections.title: Tailor the page to one posting

blocks.html:
Job Bank says a good resume shows your background, skills, and qualifications, and that you should tailor it to the job by highlighting relevant accomplishments. Their “stand out” page adds that a resume should not be one size fits all. Recruiters are not helped by generic, dated, or irrelevant information.

Alis gives six steps. After you have a master resume (Lesson 4), you pick a type, tailor it, choose careful words, make it look professional, and proofread. For wording, alis notes that some employers use tracking software that looks for the same words and phrases as the posting. If the ad says “manager” and you only write “management,” the software may not treat that as a match. Study the posting and use the same keywords honestly. Do not stuff in words for work you did not do.

Keep the version you send short. Alis says 1 to 2 pages at most. Put the strongest, most relevant qualifications near the top. Use point form, a simple readable font (alis mentions examples such as Calibri, Arial, Helvetica, Times New Roman, or Courier), wide margins, and bold only to highlight a few facts such as an award. Alis says to avoid tables or columns because some screening software cannot read them well.

If the posting allows it, alis suggests submitting a Word file (.doc or .docx), because some screening software cannot read PDF files. If the posting asks for a PDF, follow the posting. *Microsoft Word Basics* can help you save or export; this lesson will not repeat those click-paths.

sections.title: Choose a layout that fits your history

blocks.html:
Alis describes three common layouts:

  • A chronological resume lists work and education from newest to oldest. It is a good choice when the job is similar to work you have done and your history is fairly consistent.
  • A functional resume focuses on skills. It may help if you have gaps in paid work — for example after travel, raising a child, or an illness — because it highlights what you can do rather than every date.
  • A combination resume leads with skills, then gives a short work history. Alis says this works well if you are changing fields.

Job Bank’s Resume Builder (opened 10 November 2026) currently describes two templates after you sign in: a traditional template for people with several years in their field and a fairly consistent history, and a template for youth or recent graduates who are starting out or have limited paid work. You pick a template, fill in the blanks (you can select pre-defined skills and duties), customize with your own words, and save more than one resume. You need a Job Bank account to use the builder; Lesson 7 covers accounts. You can also type a resume from our outline without the builder.

Be honest in every layout. Alis says not to exaggerate or misrepresent yourself — employers may check. If a template offers a duty you did not do, do not tick it just because it sounds strong. The builder is a convenience, not a reason to borrow someone else’s work history.

sections.title: Proofread, then stop adding extras

blocks.html:
Alis says a typo or messy formatting can be enough for an employer to pass you over. Read the page out loud. Use spell check, but read its suggestions: it may not know *it’s* from *its*, or *check* from *cheque*. Ask a trusted person to read it.

For the Sampletown posting, keep lines that show greeting the public, reliable weekend attendance, and setting up a room. Leave out a long story about unrelated work unless it teaches a matching skill. A two-line summary at the top can use the posting’s own words — “weekend attendant,” “greet visitors,” “community events” — if those words are true for you.

Canadian spelling belongs on a Canadian application when you are writing in your own sentences (*centre*, *practise* as a verb). Job titles and quoted posting phrases should match the employer’s wording.

Do not include a photo unless the posting clearly asks for one (this sample does not). Do not include your SIN. Save the file with a clear name such as YourName_Sampletown_resume. Then look at the page the way a tired reader would: is your name easy to see, is the most relevant work near the top, and did you leave enough white space? If a paragraph looks crowded, turn it back into short bullets. A second read the next morning, or a read from a trusted person, often catches a missing date or a repeated verb that spell check will not flag on its own.

lessons.title: Write a short cover letter or email

sections.title: A cover letter is an introduction, not a second resume

blocks.html:
Job Bank says applying involves three steps: research the company or job, create a resume, and prepare a cover letter. A cover letter is your introduction. It should be concise, well written, and tailored to that company and job. You may need a different letter for each job. It should give the employer an idea of who you are and highlight the skills you offer.

Job Bank also says a cover letter is not always required. When it is, taking time to write a good one can make a real difference. Always read the posting: our Sampletown sample asks for a resume and a short cover note by email.

Alis says a cover letter introduces you and your resume or application form. Your goal is to get the employer’s attention by showing how your skills and accomplishments make you a good fit. Study the posting and put matching skills in the letter. Research the organization’s goals or activities — if you mention one truly, you show interest. Think about how you would benefit the organization and why the work appeals to you. The letter should make the employer want to read the resume. It should not simply repeat every line already on that resume.

Longer lessons on tone, paragraph craft, and rewriting sentences belong in *Workplace Writing*. How to send a polished workplace email belongs in *Outlook and Workplace Email Habits*. A job-application cover note is this course’s task; a deeper employer package still sits here, not in Word Basics (which only helps you type and save the file).

sections.title: A simple shape that official pages agree on

blocks.html:
Job Bank’s “stand out” page (opened 10 November 2026) suggests this shape:

  • a short opening that shows interest in the job or the organization
  • your top skills that match the posting, with one or two clear examples
  • a closing that repeats your interest or thanks the reader

That is enough for a basic email. Name the job title in the first lines so a busy reader knows which posting you mean. If you know the person’s name from the posting, use it and spell it correctly (alis reminds people to do that on a master list). If you do not know a name, a simple “Hello” plus the team or “Hiring team” is safer than inventing “Dear Sir.”

Keep the note to about three short paragraphs, or a tight screen of email. Use the same keywords you used on the resume, and support them with one real example: “I greeted visitors at a volunteer skate sale” is stronger than “I am great with people.” Do not apologize for missing an optional asset unless the employer asked about it. Do not include a SIN, a photo, or a joke about being desperate for any job.

If you send the note as an email, use a clear subject such as Weekend Attendant application — Your Name. Say that your resume is attached, and attach the file you named in Lesson 5. If you type the note as a one-page letter instead, alis says to send it the way the posting asks, along with the resume.

sections.title: Tailor it, then leave it alone

blocks.html:
Write the Sampletown note for that one sample job. If you later apply to a different posting, change the title, the examples, and any organization detail you mention. Sending the same copied paragraph to every employer, including ones you did not read about, is what official pages warn against.

Read the note out loud, the same way you proofread the resume. Check that you spelled Sampletown and the job title as they appear on the posting. Check that you attached the correct file, not last year’s letter to a different place. Alis says clear file names prevent that mistake.

This note is practice. It is not a real application and not a promise anyone will reply. Do not send it to a real town office.

If writing English sentences is the hard part, ask a tutor to help you say your example out loud first, then write what you said. Workplace Writing can help with tone later. The official test of this letter is simple: would a busy reader see which job you want, why you are a reasonable match, and how to open your resume? sections.title: Follow the instructions on the posting

blocks.html:
Canada’s Skills for Success Digital skills include using online forms for things such as purchases, opening accounts, and job applications (learning-steps page, opened 10 November 2026). That is why this lesson exists: applying is often a form, an email, or an account — not only a paper resume.

Alis says employers may ask for a resume and letter (by email, a website, or in person), or for an application form that everyone fills in the same way, or for both. Read what they want. Use the format and delivery method they prefer. Apply to more than one suitable job rather than waiting to hear back from the first; many employers only contact people they plan to interview.

Keep a copy of what you sent and the date, on the master list from Lesson 1. Name the files clearly so the resume and the letter match the same employer.

If you apply by email, *Outlook and Workplace Email Habits* can help with sending and signing out on a shared computer. If you fill a web form, type only what the form asks and what you are willing to share. You can browse many Job Bank listings without an account; you need an account for extra tools. Double-check spelling of the employer’s name before you submit. A form that asks for the same facts as your resume — dates, duties, education — should match the resume you attached, so the two documents do not tell two different stories. If you are using a public computer, finish, save your own copies, and sign out of the email or Job Bank session.

sections.title: Job Bank accounts, alerts, and your SIN

blocks.html:
Job Bank’s find-a-job page (opened 10 November 2026) says a Standard account can be started with an email address. With it you can customize searches, get daily Job Alerts, and use resume templates.

A Plus account adds more tools, such as matching you with openings from a profile, invitations from employers, and applying from some postings with a saved resume or one made in the Resume Builder.

Some extra services, including Job Match and Direct Apply, ask you to confirm that you are a Canadian citizen, a permanent resident, or a temporary resident. To prove eligibility, Job Bank may ask for your date of birth, a parent’s last name at birth, and your valid Social Insurance Number (SIN). Job Bank says the SIN is checked automatically and will not be kept in its records.

If you cannot provide that information or prefer not to, Job Bank says you can still sign up by opting out of those extra services. You can add the information later if you change your mind. This course will not tell you which immigration category you are in. You should not type your SIN into this course, a quiz, or a practice file.

When a posting offers Direct Apply, follow the official steps on Job Bank and read any box that asks you to share your email and documents with that employer. Keep your Job Bank password private, just as you would for email.

If a site looks different from a practice screen, trust the live official page and a tutor, not a drawing. Job Bank account rules can change; the facts in this lesson are dated 10 November 2026. Take a breath before you submit. Reread any box that says you are about to share your email or documents with an employer. If you are not sure what a field means, leave it and ask rather than inventing an answer. You can save a draft on paper: the job title, the site you used, the files you sent, and the date. lessons.title: Prepare for an interview using official tips

sections.title: An interview is a meeting, not a verdict

blocks.html:
An interview is a meeting where an employer asks about your skills and you learn about the job. Job Bank’s stand-out page reminds people that being invited is already a step forward: you are part of a smaller group of applicants. This course still cannot promise the job.

Job Bank says to prepare in advance: research the company; think of questions they might ask and prepare answers from your work or education; use the STAR method to structure examples (Situation, Task, Action, Result); practise with friends or family; and on the day, bring copies of your resume and a list of references, and dress in a way that fits the workplace.

Alis treats an interview as a business meeting with two tasks: show that you have the skills to get the job done, and find out whether you are interested in the work. When someone calls to set up a time, you may politely ask whether it is a first screening or a hiring interview, and how many people will be there. Write down names if they offer them.

Alis’s work-search basics page also says to leave questions about pay and benefits until after they offer you the job. That is a timing tip, not a rule of law. If an interviewer raises pay first, you may listen and write the figure down later (Lesson 9). This course will not tell you what number to ask for.

sections.title: STAR, STARS, and stories you can tell honestly

blocks.html:
Job Bank’s STAR method helps you turn a memory into a clear example: what was going on (Situation), what you needed to do (Task), what you did (Action), and what happened (Result). Alis uses a similar method called STARS, which adds Skills — name the skill the story shows.

Pick examples that match the posting. For Sampletown, a useful story might be greeting a long line at a volunteer skate sale (situation), keeping the line moving without rushing people (task), calling the next person and answering where to try on skates (action), and finishing the morning without a backup at the door (result). The skill is clear, calm communication.

Write two stories on the interview practice sheet before you try them out loud. Alis says to practise by saying answers out loud, and to try a practice interview with a friend while you notice whether you sound rushed or unclear. You do not need a perfect performance. You need examples you can remember when you are nervous.

Be ready to explain a gap or a weakness without inventing a history. Alis says to be prepared to explain perceived weaknesses and the steps you have taken to address them. Honest and short is better than a long excuse.

Participate (listen, answer thoughtfully, and follow up later)

sections.title: The day of the interview, and your questions

blocks.html:
Alis’s four habits continue on the day: present yourself well — be neat, on time, and dressed in a way that fits the workplace; turn off your cellphone; greet people politely. Alis also mentions avoiding scents and waiting to sit until you are offered a chair. Participate by listening closely, answering thoughtfully, and taking brief notes if that helps you. It is all right to steer the conversation gently toward a skill the job needs.

Prepare a short list of questions for them about the work itself — for example, what a typical Saturday looks like, or how new attendants learn the closing checklist. Alis says always to word questions politely. Alis’s *Work Search Basics* page also says to leave questions about pay and benefits until after they offer you the job.

Alis also says you should understand your rights about what kinds of questions are appropriate, and the work-search basics page notes that some personal questions are not allowed. This course is not legal advice and will not give you a full list of prohibited questions. If a question worries you, you may say you would like to think about it, and later ask council staff or read official human-rights information. Do not use this course as a courtroom script.

For a phone or online interview, alis says to pick a time and place where you can speak comfortably, and to have your resume, a pen, paper, and your questions nearby. Practise with the sheet rather than memorizing a speech word for word.

After the interview comes Lesson 9. Do not assume you have the job until an employer tells you when to start (alis). Keep looking at other suitable postings.

lessons.title: After the interview: thank-you notes and next steps

sections.title: Write down the interview while you remember it

blocks.html:
Alis’s page *What to Do After an Interview* (opened 10 November 2026) says that before you forget the details, you should write down what happened. Those notes help you later if you get an offer, and they help you prepare for the next interview if you do not.

Alis suggests noting the names of the interviewer or interviewers; the questions you remember; how you answered; salary figures if they brought them up; and anything else you might need if you are offered the job. Then ask yourself a few review questions: Did you arrive on time and prepared? If it was a virtual interview, did the sound and picture work? Which questions went well? Which would you answer differently next time? Did you connect your skills to what they need? What do you wish you had asked?

Do not take it personally if you do not get the job. Alis says employers often find it hard to choose among several well-qualified people. Someone else may have had more experience, the panel may already have known another candidate, or the fit may simply not have been right. Your notes are for learning, not for blaming yourself.

Keep those notes on your master list, beside the employer’s name and the interview date. If they mentioned a date by which you should hear back, write that date down too, in the same notebook as the job title.

sections.title: Send a short, specific thank-you

blocks.html:
Alis says that regardless of the outcome it is a good idea to write a brief thank-you for the interviewer’s time and consideration. It can set you apart, remind them of your strongest qualifications, and let you add a fact you missed. Like a resume or cover letter, the note should be tailored: mention something specific from the conversation.

Alis offers a three-part shape:

  • First paragraph: thank them for their time and for telling you about the organization and the position.
  • Middle paragraph: note what you learned, remind them why you are a good fit, and mention any qualification you did not have time to cover. If they raised a concern, you may address it briefly and honestly.
  • Final paragraph: confirm that you are still interested.

You can send the note by email so it arrives quickly. Alis says you may also follow up by regular mail, and that a handwritten note is fine if your writing is easy to read. For most learners in this course, a short email the same day or the next day is enough.

Alis’s interview-preparation page also suggests a thank-you note or email that names two or three reasons you are a good fit. Use reasons you actually discussed or can support — not new inventions.

How you send email, and how you sign out on a shared computer, belongs in *Outlook and Workplace Email Habits*. The words of the thank-you are this lesson’s work.

sections.title: If you hear nothing — or you hear no

blocks.html:
If the employer named a date and you have not heard back, alis’s work-search basics page says to note the date and call if nothing arrives by then. If you promised to call on a certain day, put a reminder on your plan and keep the promise.

If there is no offer, alis lists common reasons: someone else had more experience; your answers were not complete; the interviewers wanted to hire someone they already knew; or the fit with the culture was not right. Many interviewers are willing to say why. If you ask for feedback, alis says to make it clear you are not asking them to defend the decision — you want to learn. Suggested questions include how you might improve your resume or interview skills, what you could do better, and whether there might be a future chance. Some people will not answer. Do not argue. Thank them and say goodbye.

Keep looking. Alis says not to assume you have a job until you are told when to start, and to keep following other opportunities even after interviews go well. A thank-you note is not an offer. Update your master list with the status — waiting, no, or (in Lesson 10) an offer to think about — and take care of yourself. Looking for work is tiring. A short walk or a talk with a supportive person is not a waste of the search at all.

lessons.title: Offers, pay questions, and when to ask a person for help

sections.title: An offer is more than one pay number

blocks.html:
Alis’s page *Consider These Factors Before Accepting a Job Offer* (opened 10 November 2026) says a job offer is more than a salary figure. It is a commitment that can affect your work, your household, and your well-being. It can be tempting to say yes immediately, especially if you need income soon, but alis asks you to take time to weigh the pros and cons.

Things alis invites you to consider include the base pay; whether there is room for increases; benefits you would actually use (time off, health coverage, a retirement plan, and other items they list); the work itself; how the job fits your longer plan; the people and workplace; hours and on-call expectations; travel time and cost; and whether the work is on-site, remote, or mixed. A “better” job that adds a long drive each way may not be better for your life.

Alis also asks whether the employer has given you the offer in writing. If you ask and they refuse, alis calls that a big red flag. This course will not tell you what to sign. It will tell you to read slowly, write questions down, and ask a person you trust — council staff, Alberta Supports, a settlement worker, or another official helper — before you accept something you do not understand.

Pay notes in a posting or an offer are information. They are not tax advice, payroll advice, or a lesson in *Alberta Employment Standards*. If you need to know about minimum wage, overtime, or vacation pay, use that course or official employment-standards pages, not a guess from this file.

sections.title: Questions you can write down — and ones this course will not answer

blocks.html:
You can write down, in your own words: When would I start? What are the hours? Where do I work? What does the pay include? What benefits matter to me? Are there unpaid duties that would add many hours? Is the offer in writing?

Alis says it is natural to feel pushed to accept any offer if you need a change, and asks a useful check: will this job solve the problems that made you start searching? If you are recovering from burnout, flexibility may matter more than a title. If you need a paycheque now, income may come first. Those are personal judgements, not grades in this course.

Alis notes that employers may expect some negotiation and that a first number might not be their last, and that if you are on the fence you should not be afraid to ask for something better. That is general information from their page, not a script. This course will not tell you what dollar amount to request, how to bargain, or whether you should walk away. Ask a person who knows your situation.

Do not use this course for immigration advice about whether you may accept work, or for Employment Insurance advice about leaving a job or starting a new one. Job Bank has separate information for people outside Canada; Service Canada handles SIN and EI questions. If a question is about your legal rights at work, official employment-standards or human-rights pages — or a helper at Alberta Supports (1-877-644-9992, listed on alis on 10 November 2026) — are the right next step.

sections.title: Accepting, refusing, and finishing this course

blocks.html:
Alis’s work-search basics page says an employer can withdraw an offer, even a written one, until you have accepted it. If you have more than one offer, it also says to accept the job you want, in writing, before you turn the others down. Those are official cautions, not a promise about what every employer will do. If you are juggling dates, ask a helper rather than guessing from a discussion forum.

If you say yes, alis suggests handling a resignation from a current job professionally if that applies to you. If you say no, do it politely and keep your notes — you may meet the same people again.

Then wrap up the search tools you will want next time: keep the master list up to date, keep sample thank-you wording you liked, and keep learning. Alis says work search is a skill you will likely use more than once.

Your capstone for this course is practice: one tailored resume and a short cover email for the fictional Sampletown posting, compared with the model answer. It is not graded. The final exam is a knowledge test. Passing it means you passed that exam (and you should try the capstone). It does not mean a tutor watched you apply for work, and it does not mean you will be hired. When the exam is done, you still have your master list, a sample resume, and official pages you can reopen whenever the next posting appears.
